title: Anogenital Distance Links Prenatal Hormonal Programming to Breast Cancer Risk
content: Background: Prenatal hormonal programming has been proposed as a determinant of breast cancer susceptibility, although reliable biomarkers of fetal endocrine exposure are lacking. Anogenital distance (AGD), a sexually dimorphic anthropometric measure established during fetal development, has been suggested as a surrogate marker of the prenatal hormonal milieu. We investigated the association between AGD and breast cancer occurrence in adult women and explored whether this association varied according to menopausal status, intrinsic molecular subtype, or genomic recurrence risk. Methods:  In this prospective case–control study, 422 women with newly diagnosed breast cancer and 417 cancer-free controls were consecutively recruited at a tertiary university hospital. Two AGD measurements—the ano-clitoral distance (AGDAC) and the ano-fourchette distance (AGDAF)—were obtained using a standardized protocol. Multivariable logistic regression models estimated odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) across AGD quintiles after adjustment for age and body mass index (BMI). Stratified analyses by menopausal status and exploratory analyses according to intrinsic molecular subtype and Oncotype DX® Recurrence Score were performed. Results: Women with breast cancer had significantly longer AGDAC and shorter AGDAF than controls. Increasing AGDAC was independently associated with higher odds of breast cancer, showing a significant trend across quintiles (P<0.001). This association was consistent in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women. AGD measurements were not associated with intrinsic molecular subtype or genomic recurrence risk. Conclusions: AGD was associated with breast cancer occurrence, supporting a potential contribution of prenatal developmental programming to breast cancer susceptibility. These findings warrant external validation in larger, multicenter cohorts before any clinical application.
